questions.stem: A provider orders protamine sulfate to reverse heparin therapy after a significant bleeding event, and a newer nurse begins drawing it up to give as a fast IV push to reverse the anticoagulation as quickly as possible. The nurse should instead ensure protamine is administered:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer protamine without performing any dosing calculation relative to the amount of heparin the client actually received","B":"Give protamine as a rapid IV bolus in order to achieve the fastest possible reversal, as the newer nurse was preparing to do","C":"Administer protamine only through the oral route, never by intravenous injection, despite the urgency of this bleeding event","D":"Slowly via IV per protocol, since rapid administration, like what the newer nurse was about to do, can cause hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions"}}
questions.rationale: Protamine sulfate must be administered slowly via IV per facility protocol, since rapid administration is associated with hypotension, bradycardia, and anaphylactoid reactions. Dosing is calculated based on the amount and timing of heparin given.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Protamine Sulfate Injection
questions.source_detail: Administration Rate and Adverse Reaction Risk

questions.stem: A provider orders an IV insulin infusion for a client in DKA, and a student nurse reaches for a vial of NPH insulin from the medication cart to prepare the infusion. The nurse should recognize that among insulin types, only which type is actually approved for IV administration?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Regular insulin, the only insulin type approved for IV use, unlike the NPH the student reached for","B":"An intermediate-acting insulin formulation not approved for IV administration in this or any clinical setting","C":"A newer analog insulin engineered specifically to release slowly over many hours","D":"A basal insulin with a very different onset profile that is also not cleared for IV use in this setting"}}
questions.rationale: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the only insulin type approved for IV administration. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir must never be given IV, and NPH (intermediate-acting) is also not given via the IV route, per FDA labeling and standard practice.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Regular Human Insulin

questions.stem: A new nurse asks whether IV potassium chloride can be given as an IV push for a client with severe symptomatic hypokalemia. The experienced nurse's correct response is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No, IV potassium should never be given as an undiluted IV push due to risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia","B":"Only if the client specifically requests a faster route of administration","C":"Yes, but this route is appropriate only within an emergency department setting","D":"Yes, IV push is always considered an appropriate route for severe hypokalemia"}}
questions.rationale: IV potassium chloride must never be administered as an undiluted IV push, regardless of the severity of hypokalemia, due to the significant risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmias. It must always be diluted and administered via controlled infusion, typically with cardiac monitoring for higher concentrations.
questions.source_name: ISMP — High-Alert Medications: Potassium Chloride Safety

questions.stem: A provider orders a digoxin loading dose for a client with new-onset atrial fibrillation, and the client asks why they can't just start on the same daily dose they'll eventually take long-term. The nurse understands that a loading dose is used to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fully replace the client's need for any ongoing maintenance dosing going forward after this single loading dose is given today to the client","B":"Reduce the client's overall risk of toxicity compared with standard maintenance dosing given right from the very start","C":"Eliminate the need for any further serum digoxin level monitoring once this particular loading dose has actually been given to the client","D":"Achieve a therapeutic drug level more quickly than standard maintenance dosing alone would allow, which is why it can't simply start at the eventual daily dose"}}
questions.rationale: A loading dose strategy is used for medications like digoxin, which have a long half-life, to achieve a therapeutic serum concentration more rapidly than would occur with standard maintenance dosing alone, though this approach also requires close monitoring for toxicity.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pharmacology Reference — Digoxin Loading Dose Principles

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is newly prescribed a beta-blocker for a separate cardiac condition, and mentions relying heavily on feeling their heart race or hands shake to know when their blood sugar is dropping. The nurse should teach the client that this medication may:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Have fairly little meaningful effect on the client's ability to recognize hypoglycemia symptoms the way they currently do at home","B":"Masking common early hypoglycemia symptoms like tachycardia and tremor, the very signs this client relies on, making glucose checks especially important","C":"Eliminate the client's ongoing need to perform routine blood glucose monitoring now that the beta-blocker therapy has started","D":"Guarantee that the client will never experience an episode of hypoglycemia while taking this particular new medication"}}
questions.rationale: Beta-blockers can blunt the sympathetic nervous system response to hypoglycemia, masking common warning signs such as tachycardia and tremor (though sweating typically remains). This makes regular blood glucose monitoring especially important for clients with diabetes taking these medications.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Beta-Blockers in Diabetic Patients

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing medications for a 76-year-old client with mild chronic kidney disease who takes an over-the-counter NSAID daily for joint pain without realizing it could be a concern. The nurse should recognize a particular concern with regular NSAID use in this population due to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Provide enhanced renal protection when NSAIDs are used on a chronic, ongoing basis by a client with this particular history","B":"Improve overall renal blood flow when NSAIDs are used regularly by a client with this particular medical history","C":"Present no relevant renal concern for a client with pre-existing chronic kidney disease of this particular severity level","D":"The risk of further renal impairment, since NSAIDs can reduce renal blood flow in a client with existing kidney disease"}}
questions.rationale: NSAIDs can reduce renal blood flow by inhibiting prostaglandins that help maintain renal perfusion, posing particular risk for older adults or those with existing renal impairment, who may experience further decline in kidney function with regular NSAID use.
questions.source_name: American Geriatrics Society — Beers Criteria, NSAID Use in Older Adults
questions.source_detail: Renal Risk with NSAIDs in Older Adults

questions.stem: A client taking haloperidol develops high fever, severe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. The nurse should recognize these as signs of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A simple viral illness with symptoms entirely unrelated to the client's medication","B":"A normal, expected effect of the medication requiring no further nursing action","C":"Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate medication discontinuation and supportive care","D":"An expected medication side effect that requires no further clinical intervention"}}
questions.rationale: High fever, severe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability (labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis) are the classic tetrad of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic medications requiring immediate drug discontinuation, aggressive cooling, and intensive supportive care.
questions.source_name: Cleveland Clinic / Clinical Psychiatric References — Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

questions.stem: A client who has taken a benzodiazepine daily for an extended period wants to stop the medication abruptly this weekend because they "don't feel like they need it anymore." The nurse should explain that abrupt discontinuation carries a risk of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An immediate improvement in the client's symptoms with no associated withdrawal risk from stopping this weekend","B":"No significant withdrawal effects at all when this type of medication is stopped abruptly, as the client is planning","C":"Understand that stopping this way carries fairly few withdrawal effects worth mentioning to the client","D":"Understand that stopping this way carries just mild, largely inconsequential symptoms not needing supervision"}}
questions.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation of benzodiazepines after prolonged use carries a risk of withdrawal symptoms, including anxiety, tremor, and potentially life-threatening seizures. A gradual, medically supervised taper is the recommended approach to safely discontinue these medications.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Benzodiazepines

questions.stem: A client is started on scheduled opioid therapy for chronic pain. The nurse should anticipate the provider will likely also order:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A scheduled antidiarrheal medication given prophylactically alongside the opioid","B":"A high-dose antacid medication given prophylactically alongside the opioid","C":"A stimulant laxative or stool softener as prophylaxis against opioid-induced constipation","D":"No bowel regimen at all, since constipation is considered a rare opioid side effect"}}
questions.rationale: Opioid-induced constipation is extremely common due to opioids' effect on GI motility. Prophylactic use of a stimulant laxative or stool softener (rather than waiting for constipation to develop) is standard practice when initiating scheduled opioid therapy.
questions.source_name: American Pain Society / Clinical Guidelines — Opioid-Induced Constipation Prevention
questions.source_detail: Prophylactic Bowel Regimen with Opioid Therapy

questions.stem: A client receiving IV vancomycin for a serious infection develops flushing and a rash on the face, neck, and upper torso during a rapid infusion, but blood pressure and airway remain stable. The nurse should recognize this as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"\"Red man syndrome,\" typically caused by histamine release from rapid infusion, generally managed by slowing the infusion rate rather than stopping treatment","B":"A sign that the client's vancomycin dose should be doubled right away in order to try to overcome this particular kind of reaction seen","C":"A true IgE-mediated allergic reaction requiring immediate epinephrine, given the stable vital signs actually described here","D":"An entirely unrelated skin condition with no connection at all to the vancomycin infusion the client is currently receiving"}}
questions.rationale: "Red man syndrome" is a common infusion-related reaction to vancomycin, typically caused by histamine release from rapid infusion rather than a true IgE-mediated allergy. It is generally managed by slowing the infusion rate and, if needed, giving an antihistamine, rather than discontinuing the medication entirely.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pharmacology Reference — Vancomycin Infusion Reactions
questions.source_detail: Red Man Syndrome and Infusion Rate

questions.stem: A nurse is collecting a blood culture specimen from a client with a suspected bloodstream infection, and a colleague suggests just wiping the site quickly since the client is anxious about the needle. To minimize the risk of contamination, the nurse should instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skip performing skin antisepsis, following the colleague's suggestion, in order to save time and reduce the client's anxiety","B":"Use proper antiseptic technique to thoroughly cleanse the skin site before venipuncture, despite the client's anxiety","C":"Touch the venipuncture site again with a bare finger after cleansing it, just before inserting the needle","D":"Draw the blood sample through the client's existing peripheral IV line instead, since one happens to be in place"}}
questions.rationale: Proper antiseptic skin preparation before venipuncture is essential to minimize the risk of blood culture contamination from skin flora, which can lead to false-positive results and unnecessary antibiotic treatment. Drawing through an existing line and re-touching the site after cleansing both increase contamination risk.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Standards Institute — Blood Culture Collection Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Skin Antisepsis for Blood Culture Collection

questions.stem: A nurse is obtaining a wound culture from a client with a chronic, draining leg wound that has visible dried drainage crusted around its edges. To obtain the most accurate results, the nurse should:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Swab the exudate that has already collected on the outside of the wound dressing rather than the wound itself","B":"Avoid cleansing the wound before swabbing, in order to try to capture whatever organisms happen to be present","C":"Swab just the surrounding intact skin near the crusted edges rather than the wound bed itself","D":"Cleanse the wound with normal saline first to remove the old surface debris, then swab the actual wound bed itself"}}
questions.rationale: To obtain an accurate wound culture, the wound should first be cleansed with normal saline to remove surface debris and old drainage, then the wound bed itself should be swabbed (following a specific technique, such as a zigzag pattern), rather than culturing old exudate, which may not reflect the true underlying infection.
questions.source_name: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society — Wound Culture Collection Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Proper Technique for Accurate Wound Cultures

questions.stem: After collecting a laboratory specimen, the nurse should label the specimen container:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"At the client's bedside, immediately after collection, before leaving the room","B":"Only if time happens to permit, otherwise deferring the labeling until later","C":"By asking unlicensed assistive personnel to label the specimen at a later time","D":"Later, once the nurse has returned to the nurses' station after the collection"}}
questions.rationale: Best practice for specimen labeling requires labeling the container at the client's bedside, immediately after collection and before leaving the room, to prevent mislabeling errors that could lead to serious diagnostic or treatment mistakes for the wrong client.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Patient Safety Goals: Specimen Labeling

questions.stem: Before administering a scheduled medication, the nurse checks the client's identification band and finds it has become smudged and illegible after a recent shower. The client is alert and states their name and birthdate correctly. The nurse should:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ask the family member currently at the bedside to verify the client's identity instead of replacing the band","B":"Skip identification verification for this single dose, since the client stated their name and birthdate correctly","C":"Obtain a new, correctly printed identification band before proceeding with the medication administration","D":"Proceed with administration anyway, relying on the client's assigned room number as sufficient verification"}}
questions.rationale: If a client's identification band is missing, damaged, or illegible, the nurse should obtain a new, correctly printed band and verify identity using at least two approved identifiers before proceeding with medication administration, since the ID band is a primary safety verification tool.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Patient Safety Goals: Patient Identification
questions.source_detail: Managing Missing or Illegible ID Bands

questions.stem: A nurse receives a verbal medication order from a provider over the phone during a rapidly evolving emergency, and another nurse in the room is already preparing the medication based on what they overheard. Best practice requires the ordering nurse to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Have the medication administered first by the other nurse and document the verbal order only afterward","B":"Read back the complete order to the provider for verification before the medication is actually prepared or given","C":"Ask the colleague who overheard the order, rather than the provider, to verify what was actually said","D":"Simply write down the order as heard, with no further verification step, given the urgency of the situation"}}
questions.rationale: Best practice for verbal or telephone orders includes the nurse reading back the complete order to the prescribing provider for verification ("read-back" or "repeat-back"), helping to catch and correct any miscommunication before the order is carried out, per Joint Commission safety standards.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Patient Safety Goals: Verbal Order Verification

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer IV insulin, a high-alert medication, to a client whose blood glucose was just rechecked and is trending down faster than expected. Facility policy requires:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An independent double-check by a second qualified nurse before administration, especially given the client's changing glucose trend","B":"Verification being expected mainly if the administering nurse personally feels uncertain about the dose being given","C":"No additional verification beyond what standard practice already includes for this particular medication","D":"Double-checking being expected mainly for oral medications, rather than for IV medications like the insulin being prepared here"}}
questions.rationale: High-alert medications, such as IV insulin, IV heparin, and chemotherapy agents, generally require an independent double-check by a second qualified nurse before administration, per ISMP recommendations and facility policy, given the significant potential for harm if an error occurs.
questions.source_name: ISMP — High-Alert Medications: Independent Double-Check Recommendation

questions.stem: A client is being transferred from the emergency department to an inpatient unit after being started on a new IV antibiotic and having a fall risk identified during triage. Effective transfer handoff communication in this situation should include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Just the client's newly assigned room number on the receiving inpatient unit, since other details are in the chart","B":"Current clinical status, pending results, the new antibiotic given, and the identified fall risk and any other special precautions","C":"Just the client's billing and insurance information, with fairly little clinical detail included in the verbal handoff","D":"Skipping verbal handoff communication, since the written documentation is considered sufficient on its own"}}
questions.rationale: Effective transfer handoff communication (such as using SBAR) should include the client's current clinical status, pending diagnostic results, treatments already provided, and any special precautions or concerns, ensuring continuity of safe care as the client moves between units or care teams.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Patient Safety Goals: Handoff Communication

questions.stem: A client identified as high fall risk is given a colored identification armband per facility protocol. The purpose of this practice is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Visually alert all staff to implement fall precautions","B":"Replace the need for a formal fall risk assessment","C":"Indicate the client's dietary restrictions","D":"Restrict the client's visitors"}}
questions.rationale: Color-coded identification armbands (commonly used for fall risk, allergies, or other alerts) provide a quick visual cue to all staff members, helping ensure appropriate precautions (such as fall precautions) are consistently implemented across all interactions with the client.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission / AHRQ — Fall Prevention Communication Strategies
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Fall Risk Identification Bands

questions.stem: An Advanced Practice Registered Nurse (APRN), such as a Nurse Practitioner working in a state with full practice authority, generally has an expanded scope of practice compared with a Registered Nurse, which may include:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little meaningful difference in scope of practice at all compared with a standard registered nurse working the same shift","B":"A scope of practice that is treated as identical and uniform across essentially every single U.S. state and territory","C":"Performing just tasks identical to those of unlicensed assistive personnel working on the same unit","D":"Diagnosing conditions and prescribing medications, within the specific scope defined by their state's practice authority and certification"}}
questions.rationale: APRNs, including Nurse Practitioners, generally have an expanded scope of practice that may include diagnosing conditions and prescribing medications, within the boundaries defined by their state's Nurse Practice Act and their specific certification, though the degree of independent practice authority varies by state.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — APRN Consensus Model
questions.source_detail: Expanded Scope of Practice for APRNs

questions.stem: A newly graduated nurse enrolls in a hospital's nurse residency program. The primary purpose of this program is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Reduce the new nurse's salary during the residency period with no educational benefit","B":"Benefit the hospital alone, providing no meaningful benefit to the new nurse","C":"Support the transition from student to practicing nurse through structured mentorship, education, and skill development","D":"Fully replace the clinical training the nurse already received in nursing school"}}
questions.rationale: Nurse residency programs are designed to support the critical transition from nursing student to practicing nurse, providing structured mentorship, ongoing education, and skill development during the first year of practice, which has been associated with improved retention and competence.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Credentialing Center — Practice Transition Accreditation Program
